claim: The transport of transition metal ions by members of the SLC11/NRAMP family constitutes a ubiquitous mechanism for the uptake of Fe2+ and Mn2+ across all kingdoms of life.
source: The transport of transition metal ions by members of the SLC11/NRAMP family constitutes a ubiquitous mechanism for the uptake of Fe2+ and Mn2+ across all kingdoms of life.
evidence: This is a general statement about the SLC11/NRAMP family that draws from established scientific knowledge about these transporters.

claim: Two branches of the SLC11/NRAMP family have evolved a distinct substrate preference with one mediating Mg2+ uptake in prokaryotes and another the transport of Al3+ into plant cells.
source: Despite the strong conservation of the family, two of its branches have evolved a distinct substrate preference with one mediating Mg2+ uptake in prokaryotes and another the transport of Al3+ into plant cells.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work on these branches of the family.

claim: Previous work on the SLC11 transporter from Eggerthella lenta revealed the basis for its Mg2+ selectivity.
source: Our previous work on the SLC11 transporter from Eggerthella lenta revealed the basis for its Mg2+ selectivity (Ramanadane et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: SiNRAT transports diverse divalent metal ions.
source: We show that the protein transports diverse divalent metal ions and binds the trivalent ions Al3+ and Ga3+, which are both presumable substrates.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from transport assays shown in the manuscript.

claim: SiNRAT binds the trivalent ions Al3+ and Ga3+, which are both presumable substrates.
source: We show that the protein transports diverse divalent metal ions and binds the trivalent ions Al3+ and Ga3+, which are both presumable substrates.
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC experiments and competition assays shown in the manuscript.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of SiNRAT displays an occluded conformation that is closer to an inward- than an outward-facing state.
source: Its cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structure displays an occluded conformation that is closer to an inward- than an outward-facing state, with a binding site that is remodeled to accommodate the increased charge density of its transported substrate.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from cryo-EM analysis and comparison with other structures.

claim: The binding site of SiNRAT is remodeled to accommodate the increased charge density of its transported substrate.
source: Its cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structure displays an occluded conformation that is closer to an inward- than an outward-facing state, with a binding site that is remodeled to accommodate the increased charge density of its transported substrate.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis of the binding site and comparison with other family members.

claim: Fe2+ and Mn2+ are important trace elements in biology due to their unique properties to form coordinative interactions with elements containing free electron pairs and their ability to readily change their oxidation states.
source: Owing to their unique properties to form coordinative interactions with elements containing free electron pairs and their ability to readily change their oxidation states, Fe2+ and Mn2+ are important trace elements in biology.
evidence: This is a statement based on established scientific knowledge about the properties of these metal ions.

claim: The uptake of Fe2+ and Mn2+ into cells requires an elaborate mechanism that allows their selection from a large background of alkaline earth metal ions and their efficient concentration within cells.
source: The uptake of both ions into cells requires an elaborate mechanism that allows their selection from a large background of alkaline earth metal ions and their efficient concentration within cells.
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge about the challenges of metal ion transport.

claim: Members of the SLC11 family constitute a conserved family of secondary active transporters that facilitate the cotransport of transition metal ions together with protons acting as energy source.
source: This formidable task is performed by members of the SLC11 family, which constitute a conserved family of secondary active transporters that facilitate the cotransport of transition metal ions together with protons acting as energy source (Courville et al., 2006; Gunshin et al., 1997; Montalbetti et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work on the SLC11 family.

claim: The common molecular features conferring ion selectivity and proton coupling are strongly conserved within different branches of the SLC11 family.
source: To be able to do this across all kingdoms of life, the common molecular features conferring ion selectivity and proton coupling are strongly conserved within different branches of the family (Bozzi and Gaudet, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review on the SLC11 family.

claim: NRAMP-related Mg2+ transporters (NRMTs) comprise a large group within the SLC11 family.
source: These comprise the large group of NRAMP-related Mg2+ transporters (NRMTs) and a smaller group of NRAMP-related Al3+ transporters (NRATs) (Chauhan et al., 2021; Shin et al., 2014; Xia et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work on these transporter groups.

claim: NRAMP-related Al3+ transporters (NRATs) comprise a smaller group within the SLC11 family.
source: These comprise the large group of NRAMP-related Mg2+ transporters (NRMTs) and a smaller group of NRAMP-related Al3+ transporters (NRATs) (Chauhan et al., 2021; Shin et al., 2014; Xia et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work on these transporter groups.

claim: EleNRMT has adapted its molecular architecture to facilitate Mg2+ uptake.
source: In a recent study, we have shown how NRMTs have adapted their molecular architecture to facilitate Mg2+ uptake, by characterizing a transporter from the bacterium Eggerthella lenta termed EleNRMT (Ramanadane et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The stripping of the interacting solvent is particularly costly for Mg2+ due to its small ionic radius.
source: Due to its small ionic radius, the stripping of the interacting solvent is particularly costly for Mg2+, and its transport by EleNRMT thus likely proceeds as hydrated ion retaining most of its first coordination shell.
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge about the properties of Mg2+ and inference from structural data.

claim: Transport of Mg2+ by EleNRMT likely proceeds as hydrated ion retaining most of its first coordination shell.
source: Due to its small ionic radius, the stripping of the interacting solvent is particularly costly for Mg2+, and its transport by EleNRMT thus likely proceeds as hydrated ion retaining most of its first coordination shell.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from structural data and knowledge about Mg2+ properties.

claim: EleNRMT transports Mn2+ but not Ca2+ in addition to Mg2+.
source: Besides Mg2+, the protein also transports Mn2+ but not Ca2+.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work on EleNRMT.

claim: In NRMTs, several of the residues coordinating ions in transition metal transporters of the family are exchanged, including a conserved methionine.
source: In NRMTs, several of the residues coordinating ions in transition metal transporters of the family are exchanged, including a conserved methionine, which forms coordinative interactions with transition metals while preventing the binding of alkaline earth metal ions (Bozzi et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work on NRMTs.

claim: A conserved methionine in transition metal transporters forms coordinative interactions with transition metals while preventing the binding of alkaline earth metal ions.
source: In NRMTs, several of the residues coordinating ions in transition metal transporters of the family are exchanged, including a conserved methionine, which forms coordinative interactions with transition metals while preventing the binding of alkaline earth metal ions (Bozzi et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work on metal ion coordination.

claim: The reduction of the side chain volume of interacting residues in combination with small rearrangements of the backbone have increased the volume of the binding site in NRMTs to accommodate the hydrated ion.
source: The reduction of the side chain volume of interacting residues in combination with small rearrangements of the backbone have increased the volume of the binding site to accommodate the hydrated ion (Ramanadane et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work on NRMTs.

claim: Transport in EleNRMT is passive, unlike in proton-coupled family members.
source: Unlike in proton-coupled family members, transport in EleNRMT is passive with residues that have been assigned to participate in H+ transport being replaced by hydrophobic side chains (Ramanadane et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work on EleNRMT.

claim: Residues that have been assigned to participate in H+ transport in proton-coupled family members are replaced by hydrophobic side chains in EleNRMT.
source: Unlike in proton-coupled family members, transport in EleNRMT is passive with residues that have been assigned to participate in H+ transport being replaced by hydrophobic side chains (Ramanadane et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work on EleNRMT.

claim: NRATs form a small clade in plants whose evolutionary relationship to classical SLC11 transporters is much closer than prokaryotic NRMTs.
source: Besides the prokaryotic NRMTs, which constitute a large branch of the family that is distantly related to transition metal ion transporters of the same family, the NRATs form a small clade in plants, whose evolutionary relationship to classical SLC11 transporters is much closer (Ramanadane et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous phylogenetic analysis.

claim: NRATs have evolved to combat Al3+ toxicity in soil.
source: These proteins have evolved to combat Al3+ toxicity in soil (Chauhan et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work on NRATs.

claim: Al3+ as a strong Lewis acid strongly interacts with membranes to compromise their integrity.
source: As strong Lewis acid, this trivalent cation strongly interacts with membranes to compromise their integrity.
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge about the chemical properties of Al3+.

claim: NRATs were proposed to catalyze Al3+ uptake into the cytoplasm of root cells acting in concert with other proteins, which mediate the further transport into vacuoles where it is neutralized by the complexation with dicarboxylates.
source: As one of the mechanisms to neutralize the adverse effect of Al3+, NRATs were proposed to catalyze its uptake into the cytoplasm of root cells acting in concert with other proteins, which mediate the further transport into vacuoles where it is neutralized by the complexation with dicarboxylates (Xia et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work on NRATs.

claim: SiNRAT broadly transports divalent transition metal ions by a mechanism that is not coupled to protons.
source: We show that this protein broadly transports divalent transition metal ions by a mechanism that is not coupled to protons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from transport assays shown in the manuscript.

claim: SiNRAT shares the hallmarks of the SLC11 family.
source: The cryo-EM structure of SiNRAT displays a protein that shares the hallmarks of the SLC11 family.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from cryo-EM analysis.

claim: The SiNRAT structure harbors an ion binding region for Al3+ located inside an aqueous pocket.
source: This structure harbors an ion binding region for Al3+ located inside an aqueous pocket, which encompasses the predicted replacements of coordinating residues and which also contains an additional acidic amino acid that increases the negative charge density of the site to accommodate the larger net charge of the transported substrate.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from cryo-EM analysis.

claim: The ion binding region of SiNRAT contains an additional acidic amino acid that increases the negative charge density of the site to accommodate the larger net charge of the transported substrate.
source: This structure harbors an ion binding region for Al3+ located inside an aqueous pocket, which encompasses the predicted replacements of coordinating residues and which also contains an additional acidic amino acid that increases the negative charge density of the site to accommodate the larger net charge of the transported substrate.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data and inference about the role of the acidic residue.

claim: Seven homologues of the prototypic NRAT1 from Oryza sativa were identified in Blast searches of eukaryotic sequence databases.
source: In the course of a previous phylogenetic analysis, we were able to spot seven homologues of the prototypic NRAT1 from Oryza sativa (XP_015625418.1, Uniprot: Q6ZG85) in Blast searches of eukaryotic sequence databases (Ramanadane et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: All identified NRAT proteins contain the described hallmarks of NRATs, which distinguishes this clade of the SLC11 family from the bulk of transition metal ion transporters.
source: All identified proteins contain the described hallmarks of NRATs, which distinguishes this clade of the SLC11 family from the bulk of transition metal ion transporters (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Differences in NRATs include variations in the putative ion coordinating site, where the conserved DPGN motif on α1 of classical NRAMPs is changed to DPSN.
source: Differences include variations in the putative ion coordinating site, where the conserved DPGN motif on α1 of classical NRAMPs is changed to DPSN and the A/CxxM motif on α6 to AxxT (Lu et al., 2018; Ramanadane et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work on NRATs.

claim: The A/CxxM motif on α6 of classical NRAMPs is changed to AxxT in NRATs.
source: Differences include variations in the putative ion coordinating site, where the conserved DPGN motif on α1 of classical NRAMPs is changed to DPSN and the A/CxxM motif on α6 to AxxT (Lu et al., 2018; Ramanadane et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work on NRATs.

claim: The conserved methionine in classical NRAMPs is replaced with a threonine in NRATs, which offers a hard oxygen ligand for metal ion interactions.
source: Latter replaces the conserved methionine, whose sulfur atom is involved in transition metal ion coordination, with a threonine, which offers a hard oxygen ligand for metal ion interactions.
evidence: This statement is based on inference from sequence analysis and knowledge of coordination chemistry.

claim: SiNRAT from S. italica was selected as the biochemically best behaving homologue based on the monodispersity of the eluted peak in fluorescence size exclusion chromatography.
source: These experiments have singled out the protein from S. italica (termed SiNRAT, XP_004952002.1) as construct with comparably high expression level and promising biochemical behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from fluorescence size exclusion chromatography.

claim: SiNRAT was purified in the detergent n-dodecyl-β-D-maltopyranoside (DDM).
source: We have subsequently scaled up the expression of SiNRAT in suspension culture and purified it in the detergent n-dodecyl-β-D-maltopyranoside (DDM) for further studies (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, B.

claim: SiNRAT-mediated Mn2+ transport saturates with an apparent Km of about 14 µM.
source: Transport is strongly dependent on the Mn2+ concentration and saturates with an apparent Km of about 14 µM, reflecting the binding of the transported substrate to a saturable site (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from transport assays shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: Ca2+ and Mg2+ show concentration-dependent competition with Mn2+ transport by SiNRAT, which is indicative for their specific binding to the protein.
source: We subsequently investigated impairment of Mn2+ transport by the alkaline earth metal ions Ca2+ and Mg2+ and found a concentration-dependent competition by both ions, which is indicative for their specific binding to the protein (Figure 1C and D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from competition assays shown in the figures.

claim: SiNRAT mediates the uptake of Ca2+ and Mg2+ into proteoliposomes.
source: To investigate whether they would also be transported, we directly monitored their influx into proteoliposomes employing the fluorophores Fura-2 for the detection of Ca2+ and Magnesium Green for Mg2+. In both cases, we found a weak signal that saturates at µM concentrations, which reflects uptake of both ions (Figure 1E and F, Figure 1—figure supplement 2E-H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from transport assays shown in the figures.

claim: SiNRAT acts as uncoupled transporter that facilitates the bidirectional transport of metal ions with poor selectivity.
source: These findings suggest that, akin to the Mg2+ transporter EleNRMT, SiNRAT acts as uncoupled transporter that facilitates the bidirectional transport of metal ions with poor selectivity.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data showing lack of proton coupling.

claim: All transport experiments with SiNRAT were carried out at neutral pH.
source: Although, in a physiological context, SiNRAT presumably operates at mildly acidic extracellular conditions (i.e. at a pH <5.5), all transport experiments were carried out at neutral pH since this resulted in maximum proteoliposome stability and highest sensitivity of the employed fluorophores.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental conditions used in the study.

claim: Ga3+ inhibits Mn2+ transport by SiNRAT, which emphasizes its interaction with the transporter.
source: In an assay to investigate the interference with Mn2+ transport, we found an inhibition by Ga3+, which emphasizes its interaction with the transporter (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from competition assays shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Ga3+ does not act as non-specific inhibitor of the SLC11 family, as it did not show competition with the prokaryotic transition metal ion transporter EcoDMT.
source: Conversely, we did not observe such competition with the prokaryotic transition metal ion transporter EcoDMT, excluding the action of Ga3+ as non-specific inhibitor of the family (Figure 1—figure supplement 2I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from competition assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2I.

claim: ITC experiments showed a specific signal upon Al3+ titration as a consequence of its interaction with SiNRAT.
source: Since equivalent studies with Al3+ are prevented by its disruptive properties on membrane integrity, we used isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) to investigate the binding of the ion to SiNRAT in detergent solution. These experiments showed a specific signal upon Al3+ titration as a consequence of its interaction with the transporter (Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ITC experiments shown in Figure 1H.

claim: At neutral pH, trivalent Al3+ is at equilibrium with its hydroxyl complexes, which complicates data analysis.
source: However, at the neutral pH of the sample, the trivalent ion is at equilibrium with its hydroxyl complexes, which complicates data analysis (Kiss, 2013).
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge about Al3+ chemistry, supported by a citation.

claim: The ITC thermograms for Al3+ binding to SiNRAT were best fitted to a sum of two binding constants, both in the low micromolar range.
source: The thermograms were thus best fitted to a sum of two binding constants, both in the low micromolar range (Figure 1I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ITC experiments shown in Figure 1I.

claim: No evidence for metal ion concentration-dependent decrease of ACMA fluorescence was detected for SiNRAT with Mn2+, Ca2+, Mg2+ or Ga3+, suggesting that SiNRAT acts as uncoupled transporter.
source: To this end, we have assayed the import of H+ at increasing concentrations of the transported ions Mn2+, Ca2+, Mg2+ and the putative substrate Ga3+ but did in no case detect evidence for metal ion concentration-dependent decrease of ACMA fluorescence, despite the negative membrane potential established by an outwardly directed K+ gradient, which would facilitate H+ transport (Figure 1K and L, Figure 1—figure supplement 2J, K).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from proton transport assays shown in the figures.

claim: The nanobody Nb1SiNRAT inhibits Mn2+ transport in a concentration-dependent manner when added to the outside of liposomes.
source: The procedure allowed the identification of the nanobody Nb1SiNRAT (short Nb1) as promising interaction partner that does not dissociate during size exclusion chromatography, and which inhibits Mn2+ transport in a concentration-dependent manner when added to the outside of liposomes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from transport assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The incomplete inhibition of transport by Nb1 presumably reflects the mixed distribution of reconstituted SiNRAT residing in either inside-out or outside-out orientation.
source: The incomplete inhibition of transport by Nb1 presumably reflects the mixed distribution of reconstituted SiNRAT residing in either inside-out or outside-out orientation, where the epitopes recognized by the nanobody are only accessible in one orientation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observation of incomplete inhibition.

claim: A cryo-EM density map of the SiNRAT-Nb1 complex was obtained at 3.66 Å resolution.
source: For the SiNRAT-Nb1 complex, we have prepared samples for cryo-EM. Since data recorded in the detergent DDM did not permit a 3D reconstruction at high resolution, we have reconstituted the complex into amphipols (Kleinschmidt and Popot, 2014) and collected a large dataset, which ultimately yielded a cryo-EM density map at 3.66 Å (Figure 2—figure supplements 1–3, Table 1, Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cryo-EM analysis.

claim: The sample used for cryo-EM imaging did not contain transported ions due to challenges associated with the amphipol reconstitution process.
source: Due to the challenges associated with the amphipol reconstitution process, the sample used for imaging did not contain transported ions. In case of trivalent ions this would have required a lowering of the pH to increase their solubility, which was incompatible with nanobody binding.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental conditions used in the study.

claim: The cryo-EM map of SiNRAT was of high quality and allowed the unambiguous interpretation with an atomic model revealing details of the 3D organization of SiNRAT.
source: The resulting map was of high quality and allowed the unambiguous interpretation with an atomic model revealing details of the 3D organization of SiNRAT (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by the quality of the cryo-EM map and the resulting model.

claim: The SiNRAT structure shows a protein sharing the conserved architecture of the SLC11 family with a core consisting of a pair of structurally related repeats of five transmembrane spanning segments.
source: The SiNRAT structure in complex with Nb1 is depicted in Figure 2. It shows a protein sharing the conserved architecture of the SLC11 family with a core consisting of a pair of structurally related repeats of five transmembrane spanning segments that are oriented in the membrane with opposite directions in an arrangement that was initially observed in the amino acid transporter LeuT (Yamashita et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from cryo-EM analysis and comparison with other structures.

claim: The unwound centers of the first helix of each repeat together constitute a substrate binding site in SiNRAT.
source: In this architecture, the unwound centers of the first helix of each repeat together constitute a substrate binding site (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from cryo-EM analysis.

claim: SiNRAT contains a total of 12 membrane-inserted helices akin to other eukaryotic family members and the prokaryotic EcoDMT.
source: The protein contains a total of 12 membrane-inserted helices akin to other eukaryotic family members and the prokaryotic EcoDMT (PDBID: 5M87) (Ehrnstorfer et al., 2017), whose Cα-positions superimpose with an RMSD of 2.66 Å (Figures 2B and 3A, Figure 2—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from cryo-EM analysis and comparison with other structures.

claim: The Cα-positions of SiNRAT and EcoDMT superimpose with an RMSD of 2.66 Å.
source: The protein contains a total of 12 membrane-inserted helices akin to other eukaryotic family members and the prokaryotic EcoDMT (PDBID: 5M87) (Ehrnstorfer et al., 2017), whose Cα-positions superimpose with an RMSD of 2.66 Å (Figures 2B and 3A, Figure 2—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison data.

claim: The nanobody Nb1 binds to an extended interface located at the extracellular side of SiNRAT.
source: The nanobody binds to an extended interface located at the extracellular side. These interactions involve contacts of all three CDRs of the nanobody, which bridge the core domain of SiNRAT consisting of α-helices 1–10 with α-helices 11–12 located at its periphery, thereby contacting the loops α1–2, α5–6, α7–8 and residues on α11 and burying 1682 Å2 of the combined molecular surface (Figure 2—figure supplement 4C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from cryo-EM analysis.

claim: The nanobody Nb1 interactions with SiNRAT bury 1682 Å2 of the combined molecular surface.
source: The nanobody binds to an extended interface located at the extracellular side. These interactions involve contacts of all three CDRs of the nanobody, which bridge the core domain of SiNRAT consisting of α-helices 1–10 with α-helices 11–12 located at its periphery, thereby contacting the loops α1–2, α5–6, α7–8 and residues on α11 and burying 1682 Å2 of the combined molecular surface (Figure 2—figure supplement 4C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from cryo-EM analysis.

claim: In the SiNRAT-Nb1 complex, α11 and α12 are detached from the core domain on the extracellular part in a conformation that is presumably stabilized by Nb1 binding.
source: Unlike in EcoDMT, in this complex α11 and α12 are detached from the core domain on the extracellular part in a conformation that is presumably stabilized by Nb1 binding (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 4B, C).
evidence: This claim is based on structural data and inference about the role of Nb1 binding.

claim: The SiNRAT structure resembles an inward-occluded state of the classical SLC11 transporter DraNRAMP.
source: The observed structure resembles an inward-occluded state of the classical SLC11 transporter DraNRAMP (PDBID: 8E60, DraNRAMPocc), where most of the structure retains a conformation observed in the inward-facing structure of the same protein (PDBID: 6D9W, DraNRAMPinw) except for a movement of the intracellular part of α-helix 1 (α1a), which has rearranged to close the access path to the ion binding site (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B; Bozzi et al., 2019b; Ray et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison data.

claim: The RMSD of Cα atoms upon superposition of SiNRAT with DraNRAMPocc is 1.57 Å.
source: This resemblance is reflected in an RMSD of Cα atoms of 1.57 Å upon a superposition of SiNRAT with DraNRAMPocc and 1.74 Å with DraNRAMPinw, whereas the RMSD of 2.71 Å compared to the outward-facing conformation of the same protein (PDBID: 6BU5, DraNRAMPout) is considerably larger (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison data.

claim: The RMSD of Cα atoms upon superposition of SiNRAT with DraNRAMPinw is 1.74 Å.
source: This resemblance is reflected in an RMSD of Cα atoms of 1.57 Å upon a superposition of SiNRAT with DraNRAMPocc and 1.74 Å with DraNRAMPinw, whereas the RMSD of 2.71 Å compared to the outward-facing conformation of the same protein (PDBID: 6BU5, DraNRAMPout) is considerably larger (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison data.

claim: The RMSD of Cα atoms upon superposition of SiNRAT with DraNRAMPout is 2.71 Å.
source: This resemblance is reflected in an RMSD of Cα atoms of 1.57 Å upon a superposition of SiNRAT with DraNRAMPocc and 1.74 Å with DraNRAMPinw, whereas the RMSD of 2.71 Å compared to the outward-facing conformation of the same protein (PDBID: 6BU5, DraNRAMPout) is considerably larger (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison data.

claim: The shorter α1a of SiNRAT is located closer to α6b compared to DraNRAMPinw, resulting in a narrowing of an aqueous cavity leading toward the supposed ion binding site.
source: As in DraNRAMPocc, the shorter α1a of SiNRAT is located closer to α6b compared to DraNRAMPinw, resulting in a narrowing of an aqueous cavity leading toward the supposed ion binding site, thereby separating this site from the intracellular environment (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison data.

claim: The SiNRAT structure represents an intermediate between both endpoints of a transporter, functioning by an alternate access mechanism, that is closer to an inward-facing state.
source: We thus assume that the SiNRAT structure represents an intermediate between both endpoints of a transporter, functioning by an alternate access mechanism, that is closer to an inward-facing state.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural comparison data.

claim: In the SiNRAT structure, the binding site is sealed to both sides of the membrane by a thin gate toward the inside and a thick gate toward the outside.
source: In its conformation, the binding site is sealed to both sides of the membrane by a thin gate composed of a single layer of residues (i.e. Asp 66, Asp 140, Thr 241, Tyr 243, and Thr 346) toward the inside and a thick gate (encompassing several layers of residues and spanning about 15 Å) toward the outside (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from cryo-EM analysis.

claim: Residual cryo-EM density bridging the neighboring residues Asp 66 and Ser 68 in SiNRAT presumably originates from water, Na+, or traces of divalent metal ions.
source: Although for the reasons described above, we have not explicitly added transported ions to our sample, we find residual cryo-EM density bridging the neighboring residues Asp 66 and Ser 68 which, as part of the supposed ion binding site, are both located on the unwound loop connecting α1a and α1b (Figure 4A). This density presumably either originates from water, the monovalent cation Na+ that is contained in the sample at a concentration of 200 mM, or traces of divalent metal ions found in our solution.
evidence: This is speculation about the origin of the observed density.

claim: Asp 66 is universally conserved and was shown to constitute a key component for ion coordination in the entire SLC11 family.
source: In this putative site, Asp 66 is particularly striking, since it is universally conserved and was shown to constitute a key component for ion coordination in the entire SLC11 family.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about the SLC11 family.

claim: Ser 68 is unique to NRATs and substituted by a Gly in all other members of the SLC11 family.
source: In contrast, Ser 68 is unique to NRATs and substituted by a Gly in all other members (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: In both SiNRAT and DraNRAMPocc structures, the water-filled paths to the metal ion binding site are sealed from both sides of the membrane.
source: In both structures, the water-filled paths to the metal ion binding site are sealed from both sides of the membrane and bound ions would thus be segregated from their aqueous environment, although the occlusion toward the intracellular solution is more pronounced in DraNRAMPocc (Figures 3C, 4B and C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison data.

claim: In DraNRAMPocc, the interacting transition metal ion is predominantly enclosed by protein residues except for one contact with a small pocket harboring trapped water molecules.
source: In its binding site, the interacting transition metal ion in DraNRAMPocc is predominantly enclosed by protein residues except for one contact with a small pocket harboring trapped water molecules (Ray et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work on DraNRAMP.

claim: The side chains of Asp 56 and Asn 59 on α1, in conjunction with the backbone carbonyls of Ala 53 and Ala 227, tightly surround the bound Mn2+ in DraNRAMPocc.
source: The side chains of Asp 56 and Asn 59 on α1, in conjunction with the backbone carbonyls of Ala 53 and Ala 227, tightly surround the bound Mn2+. Additionally, the thioether group of Met 230 contributes a soft ligand for ion interactions (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from DraNRAMP.

claim: The thioether group of Met 230 contributes a soft ligand for ion interactions in DraNRAMPocc.
source: The side chains of Asp 56 and Asn 59 on α1, in conjunction with the backbone carbonyls of Ala 53 and Ala 227, tightly surround the bound Mn2+. Additionally, the thioether group of Met 230 contributes a soft ligand for ion interactions (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from DraNRAMP.

claim: A water-mediated interaction with the side chain of Gln 378 on α10 completes the octahedral coordination of the ion in DraNRAMPocc.
source: Finally, a water-mediated interaction with the side chain of Gln 378 on α10 completes the octahedral coordination of the ion (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from DraNRAMP.

claim: The equivalent region to the DraNRAMP binding site in SiNRAT contains an elongated, approximately cylindrical pocket of predominant polar character that is about 10 Å long and 4–5 Å wide.
source: In contrast, the equivalent region in SiNRAT contains an elongated, approximately cylindrical pocket of predominant polar character that is about 10 Å long and 4–5 Å wide and that encloses a three times larger volume than in DraNRAMP (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from cryo-EM analysis.

claim: The pocket in the SiNRAT binding region encloses a three times larger volume than in DraNRAMP.
source: In contrast, the equivalent region in SiNRAT contains an elongated, approximately cylindrical pocket of predominant polar character that is about 10 Å long and 4–5 Å wide and that encloses a three times larger volume than in DraNRAMP (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison data.

claim: Residues of the consensus binding site in SiNRAT include Asp 66, Ser 68, and Asn 69 on α1, and Ala 238 and Thr 241 on α6.
source: Despite the inability to pinpoint the exact location of bound ions, we find residues of the consensus binding site to line about half of this pocket (Figure 4B). These include the previously mentioned Asp 66 and Ser 68, both bordering residual density in our cryo-EM data and the conserved Asn 69, all located on α1. On α6, the interacting residues include the conserved Ala 238, whose backbone carbonyl points toward the pocket and Thr 241, which replaces the conserved methionine in NRAMP transporters and whose side chain could contribute a hard ligand for either direct or water-mediated ion interactions (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from cryo-EM analysis.

claim: Thr 241 in SiNRAT replaces the conserved methionine in NRAMP transporters and could contribute a hard ligand for either direct or water-mediated ion interactions.
source: On α6, the interacting residues include the conserved Ala 238, whose backbone carbonyl points toward the pocket and Thr 241, which replaces the conserved methionine in NRAMP transporters and whose side chain could contribute a hard ligand for either direct or water-mediated ion interactions (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is based on structural data and inference about the role of Thr 241.

claim: The glutamine on α10 involved in ion binding in DraNRAMP is replaced by a serine (Ser 403) in SiNRAT, whose shorter side chain does not contact the aqueous pocket.
source: Distinct from DraNRAMP, the glutamine on α10 involved in ion binding is replaced by a serine (Ser 403), whose shorter side chain does not contact the aqueous pocket and thus would not be available for metal ion interactions.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison data.

claim: The acidic side chain of Asp 140 located on α3 in SiNRAT lines the cavity close to the predicted ion binding site.
source: Instead, we find the acidic side chain of Asp 140 located on α3 to line the cavity, close to the predicted ion binding site, at a position that contains a threonine (Thr 130) in DraNRAMP.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from cryo-EM analysis.

claim: Asp 140 is conserved in NRATs and would increase the negative charge density of the region by offering favorable coulombic interactions that stabilize the additional positive charge of Al3+.
source: This acidic side chain, which is conserved in NRATs, would increase the negative charge density of the region by offering favorable coulombic interactions that stabilize the additional positive charge of Al3+ (Figure 4B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on structural data and inference about the role of Asp 140.

claim: Besides the replacement of the conserved methionine of the transition metal ion binding site, SiNRAT has an expanded interaction region with increased polar character and negative charge density, which together may account for the altered substrate preference and stabilize trivalent cations.
source: Thus, besides the replacement of the conserved methionine of the transition metal ion binding site, we find an expanded interaction region with increased polar character and negative charge density, which together may account for the altered substrate preference and stabilize trivalent cations.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural data about the binding site.

claim: Mutation of Asp 66 or Asn 69 to alanine severely compromised transport of Mn2+ by SiNRAT.
source: Upon mutation of the residues Asp 66 or Asn 69 to alanine, we found a severely compromised transport of Mn2+, consistent with equivalent results obtained for other pro- and eukaryotic transition metal ion transporters (Figure 5B and C; Bozzi et al., 2019b; Ehrnstorfer et al., 2014; Ehrnstorfer et al., 2017; Ramanadane et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from transport assays shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: Mutation of Thr 241 to alanine or valine strongly negatively impacted Mn2+ transport by SiNRAT.
source: In this case, we have mutated the residue to alanine to truncate the side chain and valine to preserve its volume but remove its polar character. In both cases, we found a similar strong negative impact of the respective mutations on Mn2+ transport (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from transport assays shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: The mutant T241V of SiNRAT did not show any specific heat exchange upon Al3+ titration in ITC experiments, emphasizing the importance of the residue for Al3+ interactions.
source: For this residue, we were also interested in whether a mutation would affect interactions with trivalent cations and thus investigated binding of Al3+ to the mutant T241V by ITC. Unlike WT, we did not detect any specific heat exchange, which emphasizes the importance of the residue for Al3+ interactions (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ITC experiments shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The absence of a detectable signal in T241V ITC experiments underlines the correspondence of the ITC data of WT to Al3+ binding to the consensus site.
source: The absence of a detectable signal in T241V also underlines the correspondence of the ITC data of WT to Al3+ binding to the consensus site (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of WT and mutant ITC data.

claim: Mutation of Ser 68 to alanine did not have an obvious effect on Mn2+ transport by SiNRAT.
source: Finally, we have studied a mutation of Ser 68 to alanine, which concerns a residue that is unique to NRATs and which was found in the SiNRAT structure to contribute to potential ion interactions (Figure 4A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1). Unlike previous mutations, we did in this case not observe an obvious effect on Mn2+ transport, which proceeds with similar kinetics as WT (Figure 5G and H) and whose transport is competed by the addition of Mg2+ and Ca2+ in a similar manner (Figure 5I and J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from transport assays shown in Figure 5G and H.

claim: The mutant S68A of SiNRAT did not show competition by Ga3+ in transport assays.
source: Unlike WT, we did not detect a competition by Ga3+ in equivalent experiments (Figure 5K).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from competition assays shown in Figure 5K.

claim: The mutant S68A of SiNRAT did not show any indication for Al3+ interaction in ITC experiments.
source: We thus set out to investigate the binding of Al3+ by ITC but did not find any indication for its interaction with the mutant (Figure 5L).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ITC experiments shown in Figure 5L.

claim: Experiments on the SiNRAT mutant S68A showed distinct phenotypes for the interaction with di- and trivalent cations, which points toward structural differences in their coordination with more stringent requirements for Ga3+ and Al3+ binding.
source: Taken together, our experiments on the SiNRAT mutant S68A showed distinct phenotypes for the interaction with di- and trivalent cations, which points toward structural differences in their coordination with more stringent requirements for Ga3+ and Al3+ binding.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data from the S68A mutant.

claim: The broad substrate specificity of SiNRAT is consistent with previous experiments on the metal ion transporters EcoDMT and DraNRAMP and the Mg2+ transporter EleNRMT.
source: The broad substrate selectivity is consistent with previous experiments on the metal ion transporters EcoDMT and DraNRAMP (Bozzi et al., 2016; Ehrnstorfer et al., 2017) and the Mg2+ transporter EleNRMT (Ramanadane et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work on these transporters.

claim: Attempts to change the transport properties of EcoDMT, DraNRAMP, and EleNRMT by mutagenesis, while deteriorating selectivity, have usually retained the capability of mutants to permeate Mn2+.
source: Attempts to change the transport properties of these proteins by mutagenesis, while deteriorating selectivity, have usually retained the capability of mutants to permeate Mn2+ (Bozzi et al., 2016; Ramanadane et al., 2022), whose transport appears to have lower structural requirements compared to other divalent cations.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work on these transporters.

claim: The transport of Mn2+ appears to have lower structural requirements compared to other divalent cations.
source: Attempts to change the transport properties of these proteins by mutagenesis, while deteriorating selectivity, have usually retained the capability of mutants to permeate Mn2+ (Bozzi et al., 2016; Ramanadane et al., 2022), whose transport appears to have lower structural requirements compared to other divalent cations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Mn2+ transport is retained in mutants.

claim: By the placement of a methionine contributing a soft ligand for transition metal ion interaction, the substrate binding site of classical NRAMPs has evolved to prevent interactions with alkaline earth metal ions.
source: By the placement of a methionine contributing a soft ligand for transition metal ion interaction, the substrate binding site of classical NRAMPs has evolved to prevent interactions with alkaline earth metal ions (Bozzi et al., 2016; Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work and structural data.

claim: Mutation of the conserved methionine to alanine in classical NRAMPs has turned Ca2+ into a substrate without strongly affecting Mn2+ transport.
source: This is illustrated in the mutation of this residue to alanine, which has turned Ca2+ into a substrate without strongly affecting Mn2+ transport (Bozzi et al., 2016; Ramanadane et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work on NRAMPs.

claim: NRMTs transport the small alkaline earth metal ion Mg2+ by increasing the volume of their binding site to interact with the hydrated cation, without compromising Mn2+ transport.
source: Similarly, NRMTs transport the small alkaline earth metal ion Mg2+ by increasing the volume of their binding site to interact with the hydrated cation, without compromising Mn2+ transport (Ramanadane et al., 2022; Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work on NRMTs.

claim: SiNRAT appears to have evolved to transport trivalent cations without imposing a strong selection against divalent metal ions.
source: A comparable feature is observed for SiNRAT, where the protein appears to have evolved to transport trivalent cations without imposing a strong selection against divalent metal ions (Figure 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing broad substrate specificity.

claim: The evolutionary distance of SiNRAT to classical NRAMPs is much smaller than to NRMTs.
source: The SiNRAT structure has shed light into the basis for the altered selectivity of a transporter, whose evolutionary distance to classical NRAMPs is much smaller than to NRMTs (Lu et al., 2018; Ramanadane et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous phylogenetic analyses.

claim: The presumable binding region for trivalent ions in SiNRAT was assigned based on the structural equivalence to the transition metal ion transporters DraNRAMP and ScaDMT and the Mg2+ transporter EleNRMT.
source: Although, for technical reasons, our structure did not contain trivalent ions, we assigned their presumable binding region based on the structural equivalence to the transition metal ion transporters DraNRAMP and ScaDMT and the Mg2+ transporter EleNRMT (Ehrnstorfer et al., 2014; Ramanadane et al., 2022; Ray et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from structural comparison with other family members.

claim: Similar to NRMTs, and distinct from classical NRAMPs, the ion binding site of SiNRAT is embedded in a larger aqueous cavity, which offers direct metal ion interactions with protein residues and others that are mediated via hydrating waters.
source: Similar to NRMTs, and distinct from classical NRAMPs, the ion binding site of SiNRAT is embedded in a larger aqueous cavity, which offers direct metal ion interactions with protein residues and others that are mediated via hydrating waters (Figure 4B and C, Figure 6C; Ramanadane et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison data.

claim: A proposed conversion of a classical plant NRAMP facilitating the transport of transition metals by the mutation of the consensus binding motif on α1 and α6 is likely insufficient to convert the protein into an efficient Al3+ transporter.
source: In light of the described features, a proposed conversion of a classical plant NRAMP facilitating the transport of transition metals by the mutation of the consensus binding motif on α1 and α6 is likely insufficient to convert the protein into an efficient Al3+ transporter (Lu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data and comparison with previous work.

claim: A related attempt to convert Mg2+ into a transported substrate of the prokaryotic metal ion transporter EcoDMT by introducing corresponding mutations found in NRMTs was unsuccessful.
source: A related attempt to convert Mg2+ into a transported substrate of the prokaryotic metal ion transporter EcoDMT by introducing corresponding mutations found in NRMTs was unsuccessful (Ramanadane et al., 2022), which emphasizes the relevance of residues outside a narrow signature region to confer substrate selectivity.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work on EcoDMT.

claim: The unsuccessful attempt to convert EcoDMT emphasizes the relevance of residues outside a narrow signature region to confer substrate selectivity.
source: A related attempt to convert Mg2+ into a transported substrate of the prokaryotic metal ion transporter EcoDMT by introducing corresponding mutations found in NRMTs was unsuccessful (Ramanadane et al., 2022), which emphasizes the relevance of residues outside a narrow signature region to confer substrate selectivity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that mutations in the signature region were insufficient.

claim: The broad substrate specificity of SiNRAT contrasts a previous study on the prototypic transporter NRAT1 from rice which, upon overexpression in yeast, was proposed to selectively transport Al3+ but not Mn2+.
source: The observed broad substrate specificity of SiNRAT contrasts a previous study on the prototypic transporter NRAT1 from rice which, upon overexpression in yeast, was proposed to selectively transport Al3+ but not the transition metal ion Mn2+ (Xia et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison with a previous study, supported by a citation.

claim: The apparently contradicting observation between SiNRAT and NRAT1 could reflect the distinct ways of how transport was assayed in both studies.
source: This apparently contradicting observation could reflect the distinct ways of how transport was assayed in both studies.
evidence: This is speculation about the reason for the difference in observations.

claim: In light of the data, it is unclear how Al3+ transport would proceed in presence of other divalent ions.
source: Still, in light of our data it is unclear how Al3+ transport would proceed in presence of other divalent ions.
evidence: This is a statement about the uncertainty in the mechanism based on the experimental data.

claim: The findings are in general agreement with a previous proposal that the NRAT-mediated uptake of Al3+ into cells and its subsequent detoxification by complexation with organic anions and import into the vacuolar compartment would decrease its ability to interfere with cell wall integrity.
source: Despite these ambiguities, our findings are in general agreement with a previous proposal that the NRAT-mediated uptake of Al3+ into cells and its subsequent detoxification by complexation with organic anions and import into the vacuolar compartment would decrease its ability to interfere with cell wall integrity (Xia et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison with a previous proposal, supported by a citation.

claim: The study has provided the first structural insight into the transport of trivalent cations.
source: In summary, our study has provided the first structural insight into the transport of trivalent cations and it revealed the architecture of a protein that is part of the defense against Al3+ toxicity in plants, which continues to be a large challenge for farming on acidic soil.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the significance of the study.

claim: The study revealed the architecture of a protein that is part of the defense against Al3+ toxicity in plants.
source: In summary, our study has provided the first structural insight into the transport of trivalent cations and it revealed the architecture of a protein that is part of the defense against Al3+ toxicity in plants, which continues to be a large challenge for farming on acidic soil.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the significance of the study.

claim: It was previously shown that the increased expression of proteins involved in the regulation of aluminum toxicity can lead to better aluminum tolerance.
source: Since it was previously shown that the increased expression of proteins involved in the regulation of aluminum toxicity can lead to better aluminum tolerance (Maron et al., 2013), it will be interesting to investigate whether the overexpression of NRATs would increase the tolerance of plants to elevated Al3+ levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: It will be interesting to investigate whether the overexpression of NRATs would increase the tolerance of plants to elevated Al3+ levels.
source: Since it was previously shown that the increased expression of proteins involved in the regulation of aluminum toxicity can lead to better aluminum tolerance (Maron et al., 2013), it will be interesting to investigate whether the overexpression of NRATs would increase the tolerance of plants to elevated Al3+ levels.
evidence: This is speculation about future research directions.
